methods.name: block.event
methods.description: Send an input event, such as a key press or a paste, to a block.

session_id.description: The session that holds the block.

block_id.description: The block to send the event to.

type.description: The kind of event, such as key, paste, mouse, wheel, or focus.

payload.description: The event's fields. Leaving it out is the same as an empty object.

event.description: The event to send: its type, such as paste, and its payload.

validation_notes: A client may send only `key`, `paste`, `mouse`, `wheel`, and `focus` events. Every other event type is sent only by the server. A `paste` event's `payload` is `{"text": "..."}`, and a `focus` event's `payload` is `{"action": "in"}` or `{"action": "out"}`.
The event goes straight to the block, so Lua key bindings never see it. To give key bindings the first chance at a key, use `client.key` instead.
On one connection, `block.event` calls run one at a time, in order with `client.key`, so the block receives events in the order you send them.
The call returns once the block has received the event, which may be before the block has finished acting on it.

The call fails with `bad_request` if `event` is missing or its `payload` has the wrong shape for its type. It also fails with `bad_request` if `event.type` is empty, names an event only the server sends, or names an event this server doesn't know.
If the session doesn't exist, the call fails with `session_not_found`, and if `block_id` names a block that isn't in the session, it fails with `not_found`.

methods.name: block.method
methods.description: Call a method that a block provides and return its result.

session_id.description: The session that holds the block.

block_id.description: The block to call the method on.

method.description: The block method's short name, such as write or format.

args.description: The block method's own arguments. Leaving it out is the same as an empty object.

validation_notes: Send the block method's short name, such as `write`, in `method`. `help.all` lists the methods each creator's blocks provide under `block_types`, with each method's `args_schema` and `output_schema`.

Each block method can also be called by its full name, such as `com.superlogical.terminal.write`, with the same `session_id`, `block_id`, and `args`. The full name names the block's creator, so the call works only on a block that creator made. On any other block, it fails with `conflict`.
The result is the block method's own result, as its `output_schema` describes it. `block.method` has no result schema of its own.

`block.method` doesn't wait for earlier requests on the same connection, and it can run at the same time as `client.key`. If a call depends on an earlier request, wait for that request's reply first. To call a block method in order with `client.key`, such as from a key binding, use `client.action`.

If `block_id` is missing, the call fails with `bad_request`. If the session doesn't exist, it fails with `session_not_found`. If `block_id` names a block that isn't in the session, it fails with `not_found`, and if the block has no method named `method`, it fails with `method_not_found`. If `args` is missing a required field or has a value of the wrong type, it fails with `bad_request`.

methods.name: data.connect
methods.description: Get a one-time ticket for opening a data connection to a block. A data connection streams a block's content as it changes, such as a terminal's output.

session_id.description: The session that holds the block. The connection must be attached to it with session.attach or session.bootstrap.

block_id.description: The block that provides the data.

data_ref_id.description: Which of the block's data sources to open, such as terminal.

subprotocol.description: The subprotocol the data connection will use, such as rex.data.terminal.v1. If set, the ticket works only on a connection that uses it.

ticket.description: A single-use ticket to send in the HELLO message that opens the data connection. Only a data connection from the same user can use it.

expires_in_ms.description: How long the ticket stays valid after the server issues it, in milliseconds.

validation_notes: The connection must be attached to `session_id` with `session.attach` or `session.bootstrap`. `session.attach_all` isn't enough. If the connection isn't attached, the call fails with `conflict`.
To use the ticket, open a WebSocket to `/api/data` on the server and send the ticket in the HELLO message. A ticket works once, even if the handshake fails, and expires after `expires_in_ms`.
If another user presents the ticket, the data connection gets REJECT reason 0x01, as it would for an unknown ticket. The ticket is then used up, so your own data connection can't use it either.
The server checks only that `data_ref_id` is well formed. If the block has no data by that name, the server closes the data connection with WebSocket status 1008 after the handshake.

Set `subprotocol` to the subprotocol the data connection will use, such as `rex.data.terminal.v1`. The server then refuses a data connection that uses a different one with REJECT reason 0x07, before any data is sent.
If `subprotocol` is left out, the block checks the subprotocol after the handshake and closes the data connection with status 1008 if it doesn't support it.
The call fails with `bad_request` if `data_ref_id` or `subprotocol` is malformed, and with `not_found` if the block isn't in the session or has no data to offer.

methods.name: server.version
methods.description: Get the version of Rex that the server is running and how it was built.

rex_version.description: The version of Rex the server runs, as rex version prints it, such as 0.0.1780750825-g9a754d.

platform.description: The operating system and CPU the server was built for, such as darwin_arm64 or linux_amd64.

commit.description: The Git commit the server was built from. Left out when unknown.

built_at.description: When the server was built, as an RFC 3339 timestamp. Most builds record the time of their Git commit. Left out when unknown.

dirty.description: True if the server was built from source with uncommitted changes.

api_revision.description: The newest revision of the API the server supports. Left out when it is 0.

api_min_revision.description: The oldest revision of the API the server supports. Left out when it is 0.

validation_notes: A missing `api_revision` or `api_min_revision` means 0. Servers from before these fields existed leave both out.

methods.name: server.whoami
methods.description: Get how the server identified you, and the account the server runs as.

kind.description: How the server identified the client: 'peer' (Unix socket credentials), 'windows_peer' (named pipe credentials), 'tailscale' (a Tailscale login), or 'anonymous' (not identified). Show a kind you don't know by its name.

transport.description: How the client first reached Rex: 'unix', 'named_pipe', 'tcp', or 'tailscale'. A login server passes it on unchanged.

display.description: A readable name for the client, such as uid 501 or alice@example.com. It can be out of date or shared, so compare uid, sid, or user_id instead.

remote_addr.description: The client's network address. Left out when there is none, such as on a Unix socket.

uid.description: The client's Unix user ID. Only for kind peer.

gid.description: The client's Unix group ID. Only for kind peer.

pid.description: The client's process ID when it connected, for kind peer or windows_peer, if known. Process IDs are reused, so use it only for debugging.

sid.description: The client's Windows security identifier, which survives account renames. Only for kind windows_peer.

user_id.description: The Tailscale user ID that owns the client's device. Only for kind tailscale. Check tags before treating it as a person.

login_name.description: The client's Tailscale login name, usually an email address. For display only.

node.description: The name of the client's Tailscale device. Only for kind tailscale.

tags.description: The Tailscale tags of the client's device. Any tag means the client is a machine, such as a CI runner, not a person.

path.description: The route the client took to this server, for troubleshooting. Entries include 'tailscale' (built-in Tailscale), 'tailnet' and 'tailnet-serve' (the machine's own Tailscale), and 'login-server' (passed on by a login server).

principal.description: How the server identified you when your connection opened.

account.description: The operating system account the server runs as. It can differ from your own name. Left out when unknown.

validation_notes: Which fields `principal` has depends on its `kind`. A `peer` has `uid` and `gid`, and usually `pid`. A `windows_peer` has `sid`, and usually `pid`. A `tailscale` client has `user_id`, `login_name`, and `node`, plus `tags` if its device is tagged. An `anonymous` client has none of these.
The server identifies a client when its connection opens. `principal` stays the same for as long as the connection lasts.
`principal` describes a decision the server already made when it let the client in. Use it to show who is connected, not to decide what a client may do.

methods.name: session.attach
methods.description: Attach to a session: start receiving its events and get its current view.

client_id.description: This connection's client ID. It's the same for every session the connection attaches to.

revision.description: The view's revision. It goes up by one with every change, so a larger revision is a newer view of the session.

active_window_id.description: The window the session shows. Left out when the session has no windows.

focused_block_id.description: The window's focused block, which receives typing while the window is active. Left out if the window has none.

zoomed_block_id.description: The block zoomed to fill the window, if any. Layouts keep their normal sizes, so draw this block over the whole window.

kind.description: How the layer is placed: 'tiled' for the layer that fills the window, or 'floating' for a floating layer. Draw a kind you don't know as 'floating'.

bounds.description: Where the layer sits, as [x, y, w, h] fractions of the window's width and height.

rect.description: Where this node sits, as [x, y, w, h] fractions of the window's width and height.

block_id.description: The block at this node. Set only when split isn't.

split_id.description: The split's ID. It stays the same while the split exists, so you can match splits across views.

direction.description: How the space is divided: 'horizontal' puts before on the left and after on the right, and 'vertical' puts before above after. Draw a direction you don't know as 'horizontal'.

ratio.description: The fraction of the space that before gets, between 0 and 1.

before.description: The node on the left or top.

after.description: The node on the right or bottom.

split.description: How this node divides in two. Set only when block_id isn't.

layout.description: How the layer divides its space between blocks, as a tree of splits. Null when the layer is empty.

creator_name.description: The creator that made the block, such as com.superlogical.terminal.

flavor.description: The flavor the block was made from, such as com.superlogical.terminal.shell.

host_id.description: Identifies the machine and account the block runs as. If it equals your local server's host_id, the block sees the same files you do. Otherwise treat the block as remote.

owner.description: The client that owns the block. Left out when the block has no owner.

blocks.description: The blocks in the layer, in layout order. The layout field says where each one sits.

layers.description: The window's layers, from back to front. The first is the tiled layer, which holds the window's layout and fills the window.

windows.description: The session's windows, in order. Rex.app shows them as tabs in this order.

view.description: The session's view, read after the connection started receiving its events. Apply it first, then the events whose seq is higher than the response's.

validation_notes: The connection starts receiving every event from the session, including `block_event`, before the server reads `view`. Apply `view` first, then each event whose `seq` is higher than the response's `seq`, even one that arrived before the response.

Most methods that take a `session_id` work only on a connection attached to that session, with this method, `session.bootstrap`, or `session.attach_all`. On a connection that isn't attached, they fail with `conflict`.
Attaching makes the connection's client one of the session's clients. The server sends `client_connected`, and `session.list_clients` lists the client.
`data.connect`, `session.own_block`, and `session.disown_block` need this kind of attachment. Attaching with `session.attach_all` isn't enough for them.
Calling it again for the same session is safe. It returns the same `client_id` and a fresh `view`.
If `session_id` names no session, the call fails with `session_not_found`.

methods.name: session.create
methods.description: Create a session, optionally with its first windows already in it.

label.description: The session's label, up to 128 characters. Leave it out to let the server choose one, such as quiet-meadow.

window_label.description: The window's label, up to 128 characters. Leave it out for a label made from the window's ID, such as Window 89abcdef.

layout.description: The blocks to create in the window and how to arrange them. Required. Each node holds either block, with a flavor and optional options and label, or split, with direction, before, after, and an optional ratio.

initial_windows.description: Windows to create with the session, in order. The last one becomes the active window. If any of them fails, the server creates no session.

block_ids.description: The new blocks' IDs, in layout order: each split's before side comes ahead of its after side.

revision.description: The session's revision after the window was created.

initial_windows.description: The windows created with the session, in the order requested.

validation_notes: Every argument is optional. With none, the server creates a session with no windows.
If `label` is left out or empty, the server picks one that no other session has, such as `quiet-meadow`.

The server sends `session_created` only once every window in `initial_windows` is ready, so no client sees a half-built session. If any window fails, the server closes the session and its blocks, and the call fails.
The calling client becomes the owner of every block in the initial windows.
The call doesn't attach the connection to the new session. Call `session.attach` to receive its events.
If a layout is malformed, the call fails with `bad_request` before any block is created. A flavor that no creator provides fails with `not_found`.
If the server already has as many sessions as it allows, the call fails with `conflict`.

methods.name: session.list
methods.description: List the sessions on the server.

sessions.description: Every session on the server. New sessions go at the end, and session.move changes the order.

validation_notes: Sessions are listed in the order they were created, until `session.move` changes that order. `session.attach_all` and `session.bootstrap` list them in the same order.

methods.name: session.own_block
methods.description: Claim blocks for the calling client. The result lists each block's owner.

block_ids.description: The blocks to claim. Leave it out or empty to claim every block in the session.

mode.description: How to claim them. 'take' makes the calling client the owner right away. 'request' makes it the owner only of blocks that have none, and it may get the rest when their owner gives them up or leaves. Defaults to take.

owner.description: The client that owns the block. Left out when the block has no owner.

blocks.description: Each claimed block and its owner after this call.

validation_notes: When the clients attached to a session want different things for a block, such as a terminal's size, the block follows its owner. Owning a block gives no other rights over it.
The calling client must be attached to the session, with `session.attach` or `session.bootstrap`. A connection that only called `session.attach_all` fails with `bad_request`.

Either mode puts the caller in line for the block. When the owner gives it up, detaches, or loses its connection, the block passes to the connected client in line that claimed it most recently, with any `take` ahead of every `request`.
An owner whose connection drops gets each of its blocks back when it reconnects, unless that block's owner has changed again since.
`blocks` lists each block's owner after the call, in the order of `block_ids`, with a repeated ID listed once. When you claim every block, they are sorted by `block_id`.
Every change of owner sends `block_owner_changed`. If a block in a window changes owner, the call also sends one `session_view_changed`, because `session.view` shows owners.
A `mode` other than `take` or `request` fails with `bad_request`.
If any ID in `block_ids` isn't a block in the session, the call fails with `bad_request` and changes nothing.

methods.name: session.view
methods.description: Get the session's windows, their layouts, and their blocks in one snapshot.

revision.description: The view's revision. It goes up by one with every change, so a larger revision is a newer view of the session.

active_window_id.description: The window the session shows. Left out when the session has no windows.

focused_block_id.description: The window's focused block, which receives typing while the window is active. Left out if the window has none.

zoomed_block_id.description: The block zoomed to fill the window, if any. Layouts keep their normal sizes, so draw this block over the whole window.

kind.description: How the layer is placed: 'tiled' for the layer that fills the window, or 'floating' for a floating layer. Draw a kind you don't know as 'floating'.

bounds.description: Where the layer sits, as [x, y, w, h] fractions of the window's width and height.

rect.description: Where this node sits, as [x, y, w, h] fractions of the window's width and height.

block_id.description: The block at this node. Set only when split isn't.

split_id.description: The split's ID. It stays the same while the split exists, so you can match splits across views.

direction.description: How the space is divided: 'horizontal' puts before on the left and after on the right, and 'vertical' puts before above after. Draw a direction you don't know as 'horizontal'.

ratio.description: The fraction of the space that before gets, between 0 and 1.

before.description: The node on the left or top.

after.description: The node on the right or bottom.

split.description: How this node divides in two. Set only when block_id isn't.

layout.description: How the layer divides its space between blocks, as a tree of splits. Null when the layer is empty.

creator_name.description: The creator that made the block, such as com.superlogical.terminal.

flavor.description: The flavor the block was made from, such as com.superlogical.terminal.shell.

host_id.description: Identifies the machine and account the block runs as. If it equals your local server's host_id, the block sees the same files you do. Otherwise treat the block as remote.

owner.description: The client that owns the block. Left out when the block has no owner.

blocks.description: The blocks in the layer, in layout order. The layout field says where each one sits.

layers.description: The window's layers, from back to front. The first is the tiled layer, which holds the window's layout and fills the window.

windows.description: The session's windows, in order. Rex.app shows them as tabs in this order.

validation_notes: `revision` starts at zero for a new session and goes up by one each time the view changes. Compare revisions only within one session, and keep the view with the highest revision.

A `session_view_changed` event carries only the new revision, not the view. These events can arrive out of revision order, so call `session.view` only when an event's revision is higher than the one in the view you hold.
`window_created`, `window_closed`, `window_label_changed`, `active_window_changed`, and `session_label_changed` arrive before the `session_view_changed` event for the same change.
The view holds only blocks that are in a window. `session.list_blocks` also lists detached blocks.
The view describes structure, not content. To read what a block shows, call one of its own methods, such as `com.superlogical.terminal.format`.

methods.name: blob_read
methods.description: Read a result that was too large for one reply or event, such as the output of format with max_bytes set, or a selection_copied event without text. The server keeps each result for about five minutes.

id.description: The result to read, from the reply or event that named it, such as the id in a format reply or a selection_copied event. Zero or left out reads the newest result, whatever produced it. If the server no longer has the result, the call fails with not_found.

offset.description: Where to start reading, in bytes from the start of the result. To read the next part, add the length in bytes of the data you received. Must not be negative.

max_bytes.description: The most bytes of data to return, measured once it is encoded as a JSON string. Zero or left out means 49152 (48 KiB), and values above 983040 (960 KiB) are lowered to that. Must not be negative.

id.description: The result that was read. Send it in later requests so that every part comes from the same result.

data.description: The text read, starting at offset. It never ends partway through a character. It can be shorter than max_bytes even when more text remains.

total.description: The length of the whole result, in bytes.

eof.description: True if data reaches the end of the result.

validation_notes: Call it as `com.superlogical.terminal.blob_read` with `session_id`, `block_id`, and this method's own arguments under `args`.

methods.name: clear
methods.description: Clear the screen and scrollback, keeping the current line at the top. It changes nothing while a full-screen program, such as an editor, is running.

actions.name: clear
actions.title: Clear Terminal
actions.description: Clear the screen and scrollback, keeping the current line.
actions.keywords: terminal clear screen scrollback erase cmd+k ctrl+l

validation_notes: Call it as `com.superlogical.terminal.clear` with `session_id`, `block_id`, and this method's own arguments under `args`.

methods.name: clipboard_read
methods.description: Read text that a program in the terminal copied to the clipboard. The server keeps each copy for about a minute, so a client can read text too large to send in an event.

id.description: The copy to read, from a clipboard_written event or an earlier reply. Zero or left out reads the newest copy. If the server no longer has the copy, the call fails with not_found.

offset.description: Where to start reading, in bytes from the start of the text. To read the next part, add the length in bytes of the data you received. Must not be negative.

max_bytes.description: The most bytes of data to return, measured once it is encoded as a JSON string. Zero or left out means 49152 (48 KiB), and values above 983040 (960 KiB) are lowered to that. Must not be negative.

id.description: The copy that was read. Send it in later requests so that every part comes from the same copy.

data.description: The text read, starting at offset. It never ends partway through a character. It can be shorter than max_bytes even when more text remains.

total.description: The length of the whole copied text, in bytes.

eof.description: True if data reaches the end of the text.

validation_notes: Call it as `com.superlogical.terminal.clipboard_read` with `session_id`, `block_id`, and this method's own arguments under `args`.

methods.name: format
methods.description: Get the screen and scrollback as plain text, HTML, or escape sequences.

format.description: The format to return: 'text' for plain text, 'html' for HTML with inline styles, or 'vt' for escape sequences that redraw the screen with its colors and styles. Defaults to 'text'.

trim.description: Remove spaces from the end of each line.

unwrap.description: Join lines that the terminal wrapped because they were too long, so each line of output is one line the program wrote.

extra_charsets.description: Include the selected character sets. Only used with the vt format.

extra_cursor.description: Include the cursor position. Only used with the vt format.

extra_hyperlink.description: Include the hyperlink in effect at the cursor. Only used with the vt format.

extra_keyboard.description: Include keyboard modes such as modifyOtherKeys. Only used with the vt format.

extra_kitty_keyboard.description: Include the state of the Kitty keyboard protocol. Only used with the vt format.

extra_modes.description: Include terminal modes that differ from their defaults. Only used with the vt format.

extra_palette.description: Include the color palette. Only used with the vt format.

extra_protection.description: Include the character protection mode. Only used with the vt format.

extra_pwd.description: Include the reported working directory. Only used with the vt format.

extra_scrolling_region.description: Include the scrolling region. Only used with the vt format.

extra_style.description: Include the text style in effect at the cursor. Only used with the vt format.

extra_tabstops.description: Include the tab stops. Only used with the vt format.

max_bytes.description: The most bytes of content to return, measured once it is encoded as a JSON string. If more output remains, the reply has an id, and you read the rest with blob_read. Values above 983040 (960 KiB) are lowered to that. Zero or left out returns the whole output in one reply, and the call fails with too_large if the output doesn't fit. Must not be negative.

content.description: The screen and scrollback in the requested format. If id is set, this is only the first part.

id.description: Set only when more output remains. To read the rest, call blob_read with this id and with offset set to the length of content in bytes. A reply without id holds the whole output.

total.description: The length of the whole output in bytes. Sent only when the request set max_bytes, and left out when it is 0.

eof.description: True if content is the whole output. Sent only when the request set max_bytes. Older servers never send it, so check id instead to tell whether more output remains.

validation_notes: Call it as `com.superlogical.terminal.format` with `session_id`, `block_id`, and this method's own arguments under `args`.

methods.name: input_mode
methods.description: Get how the terminal handles typed input, such as whether it is echoed. On Windows the call fails with not_found.

echo.description: True if typed characters appear on the screen. A program usually turns this off while it reads a password.

canonical.description: True if input reaches the program a line at a time, with backspace and similar keys handled before the program sees it.

signals.description: True if keys such as Ctrl+C and Ctrl+Z send signals to the foreground process instead of reaching it as input.

validation_notes: Call it as `com.superlogical.terminal.input_mode` with `session_id`, `block_id`, and this method's own arguments under `args`.

methods.name: list_dir
methods.description: List the subdirectories of a directory, and optionally its files. A relative path or ~ is resolved the way a program in the terminal would resolve it.

path.description: The directory to list: an absolute path, ~ or a path under ~/ for the home directory, or a path relative to the working directory of the terminal's foreground process. Empty lists that working directory.

prefix.description: Keep only entries whose names start with this text, ignoring case. Use it to narrow a listing that came back truncated.

limit.description: The most entries to return. Zero, negative, or left out means 2000.

files.description: Include entries that aren't directories, such as files, and mark each with file set to true.

path.description: The directory that was listed, as an absolute path. It is set even when the directory couldn't be read.

home.description: The home directory of the terminal's program. Empty if the server can't tell.

status.description: Whether the directory could be read: 'ok', 'missing' (it doesn't exist), 'not_dir' (it, or a directory on its path, isn't a directory), or 'denied' (the server isn't allowed to read it).

name.description: The entry's name within the directory.

symlink.description: True if the entry is a symbolic link. A link that leads nowhere is left out of the listing.

file.description: True if the entry isn't a directory, or is a link to something that isn't. Only set when the request sets files.

entries.description: The matching entries, hidden ones included, in the order the filesystem returns them. Sorting and hiding are up to the client. Empty unless status is 'ok'.

truncated.description: True if some matching entries were left out because the listing reached limit or grew too large for one reply. To see the rest, list again with a prefix.

validation_notes: Call it as `com.superlogical.terminal.list_dir` with `session_id`, `block_id`, and this method's own arguments under `args`.

methods.name: modes
methods.description: List the terminal modes that programs can turn on, such as the alternate screen, bracketed paste, and mouse reporting, with each mode's name, number, and whether it is on. It doesn't wake an idle terminal.

screen.description: Which screen the terminal shows: 'primary', or 'alternate' while a full-screen program such as an editor has switched to it with mode 47, 1047, or 1049. Treat any other value as 'primary'.

name.description: The mode's name, as Ghostty names it, such as 'bracketed_paste' or 'alt_screen_save_cursor_clear_enter'.

number.description: The number a program sends to set or reset the mode, such as 2004 for bracketed paste.

ansi.description: True for an ANSI mode, which a program sets with ESC [ number h. Left out for a DEC private mode, which a program sets with ESC [ ? number h. The two kinds are numbered separately, so the same number can name one mode of each kind.

set.description: True if the mode is on.

default.description: True if the mode is on in a new terminal and after a reset. Left out if it is off. A mode whose set differs from its default was changed by a program.

modes.description: Every mode the terminal tracks, ANSI modes first, each group by number. Newer servers can add modes, so look modes up by name or number and skip any you don't know.

validation_notes: Call it as `com.superlogical.terminal.modes` with `session_id`, `block_id`, and this method's own arguments under `args`.

methods.name: process
methods.description: Get the processes running in the terminal and how its program exited.

exit_code.description: The program's exit code, or -1 if it has none, as when a signal ended it.

error.description: Why the program failed, such as 'exit status 1'. Left out when it exited successfully.

last_exit.description: How the terminal's program exited. Null while it is still running, and for a terminal that didn't start a program of its own.

user_id.description: The user ID the process runs as on Unix, which shows when a command runs as another user, such as with sudo. Zero on Windows.

user.description: The name of the account the process runs as. Left out if it can't be looked up.

name.description: The file name of the executable, such as zsh. When path is left out, the system's own name for the process, which Linux limits to 15 bytes. To label a process, use the first of script, argv0, and name that is present.

path.description: The absolute path of the executable, with symlinks resolved. Left out if it can't be read, as for another user's process on Linux.

invoked_path.description: The absolute path the executable was started through, before symlinks were resolved, such as a link in a bin directory. Present only when Rex can confirm it leads to the same file as path.

argv0.description: The first argument as the process shows it now, such as -zsh for a login shell, cut to 256 bytes. Rex never returns the other arguments, because they can hold secrets.

script.description: For an interpreter such as node or python, the absolute path of the script it is running, as the user named it. Left out for other programs.

cwd.description: The process's working directory, as an absolute path. Left out if it can't be read, as for another user's process.

child.description: The process the terminal started, usually a shell. On macOS a login shell runs under login, and this describes login. Left out if there is no such process or it can't be read.

user_id.description: The user ID the process runs as on Unix, which shows when a command runs as another user, such as with sudo. Zero on Windows.

user.description: The name of the account the process runs as. Left out if it can't be looked up.

cwd.description: The process's working directory, as an absolute path. Left out if it can't be read, as for another user's process.

foreground.description: The process in the foreground, such as the shell at its prompt or the command it is running. For a wrapper such as sudo, git, or cargo, it is the command the wrapper runs. Left out if it can't be found or read.

user_id.description: The user ID the process runs as on Unix, which shows when a command runs as another user, such as with sudo. Zero on Windows.

user.description: The name of the account the process runs as. Left out if it can't be looked up.

script.description: For an interpreter such as node or python, the absolute path of the script it is running, as the user named it. Left out for other programs.

cwd.description: The process's working directory, as an absolute path. Left out if it can't be read, as for another user's process.

ancestors.description: The processes between foreground and child, nearest first: the parent of foreground, then its parent, and so on, ending with child. Left out when foreground is child, when there are more than 16, or when one of them has exited.

home.description: The home directory that the terminal's program inherited, for showing and expanding ~ in paths.

validation_notes: Call it as `com.superlogical.terminal.process` with `session_id`, `block_id`, and this method's own arguments under `args`.

methods.name: program_status
methods.description: List the status that programs in the terminal have reported. Programs report a status, such as working or blocked, with OSC 7501 escape sequences.

id.description: The record's ID. A slash separates a parent from a child, as in build/test. Left out for the root record, which holds the reports that give no ID.

state.description: What the program says it is doing: 'idle', 'working', 'done', 'blocked' (waiting for the user), or 'error'. Treat a value you don't know as 'idle'.

kind.description: What a blocked program is waiting for: 'permission', 'question', or 'auth' (a password or other credential). Left out if the program didn't say. Treat a value you don't know as if it were left out.

progress.description: How far along the program is, as a percentage from 0 to 100. Only working and blocked records have one, and only if the program reported it.

app.description: The program's name, such as cargo or terraform, exactly as it reported it.

effective_app.description: The name of the program the record belongs to: app if it is set, or else the app of the nearest parent record that has one. Left out if no record in the chain has an app.

title.description: A short label for the record, such as the name of a task. It comes from the program, so show it as plain text.

msg.description: One line of text describing the status. Show it as plain text. A client may shorten it but shouldn't try to interpret it.

updated_at.description: When the report arrived, by the server's clock, as an RFC 3339 timestamp.

name.description: The process's name, found the same way as name in the result of process. Compare it as well as pid, because the system reuses process IDs.

owner.description: The terminal's foreground process when the report arrived. Left out if the server couldn't tell.

records.description: Every record, sorted by id. The root record comes first, and each parent comes before its children. Empty if no program has reported a status.

validation_notes: Call it as `com.superlogical.terminal.program_status` with `session_id`, `block_id`, and this method's own arguments under `args`.

methods.name: pwd
methods.description: Get the working directory that a program in the terminal last reported. To find where each process actually is, call process instead.

pwd.description: The reported directory: a file:// URL when the program used OSC 7, or a plain path otherwise. Left out if no directory has been reported or a reset cleared it.

name.description: The process's name, found the same way as name in the result of process. Compare it as well as pid, because the system reuses process IDs.

owner.description: The process that reported the directory. Left out if pwd is left out or the server couldn't tell.

validation_notes: Call it as `com.superlogical.terminal.pwd` with `session_id`, `block_id`, and this method's own arguments under `args`.

methods.name: reset
methods.description: Reset the terminal to its starting state and clear the screen and scrollback. The program keeps running, and the size and default colors stay the same.

actions.name: reset
actions.title: Reset Terminal
actions.description: Return the terminal to its starting state and clear the screen and scrollback.
actions.keywords: terminal reset clear scrollback emulator can ris

validation_notes: Call it as `com.superlogical.terminal.reset` with `session_id`, `block_id`, and this method's own arguments under `args`.

methods.name: resize
methods.description: Request a terminal size in columns and rows. It applies at once if the caller owns the block or no client does, and otherwise when the caller becomes the owner.

columns.description: The width in columns, that is, characters per line, from 1 to 65535.

rows.description: The height in rows, from 1 to 65535.

cell_width_px.description: The width of one character cell in pixels, from 1 to 65535. Send it together with cell_height_px, or leave both out to keep the current cell size.

cell_height_px.description: The height of one character cell in pixels, from 1 to 65535. Send it together with cell_width_px, or leave both out to keep the current cell size.

validation_notes: Call it as `com.superlogical.terminal.resize` with `session_id`, `block_id`, and this method's own arguments under `args`.

methods.name: set_theme
methods.description: Replace the terminal's default colors. As with resize, they apply at once if the caller owns the block or no client does, and otherwise when the caller becomes the owner.

foreground.description: The default text color, as hex RRGGBB or #RRGGBB, such as #d6deeb. Empty or left out uses the built-in color.

background.description: The default background color, as hex RRGGBB or #RRGGBB, such as #011627. Empty or left out uses the built-in color.

cursor.description: The cursor color, as hex RRGGBB or #RRGGBB, such as #80a4c2. Empty or left out uses the built-in color.

palette.description: Changes to the 256-color palette, each written as index=RRGGBB or index=#RRGGBB with an index from 0 to 255, such as 1=#ef5350. Colors not listed keep their built-in values.

scheme.description: Whether the theme is 'light' or 'dark', which programs in the terminal can ask for. If empty, the terminal decides from how bright background is, and treats no background as dark.

validation_notes: Call it as `com.superlogical.terminal.set_theme` with `session_id`, `block_id`, and this method's own arguments under `args`.

methods.name: size
methods.description: Get the terminal's size, its owner, and the size each client last requested.

cell_width_px.description: The width of one character cell in pixels.

cell_height_px.description: The height of one character cell in pixels.

owner.description: The client that owns the block, whose size the terminal uses. Null if the block has no owner.

client_id.description: The client that requested this size.

updated_at.description: When the server received the request, as an RFC 3339 timestamp.

desired.description: The last size each client requested, the owner's included, newest first.

validation_notes: Call it as `com.superlogical.terminal.size` with `session_id`, `block_id`, and this method's own arguments under `args`.

methods.name: title
methods.description: Get the terminal's title and the process that set it.

title.description: The terminal's title, as a program last set it. Empty if no title is set.

name.description: The process's name, found the same way as name in the result of process. Compare it as well as pid, because the system reuses process IDs.

owner.description: The process that set the title, as title_changed reported it. Left out if no title is set, a reset cleared it, or the server couldn't tell.

validation_notes: Call it as `com.superlogical.terminal.title` with `session_id`, `block_id`, and this method's own arguments under `args`.

methods.name: write
methods.description: Type text into the terminal as if the user had typed it. The call returns once the text is queued, without waiting for the program to read it.

data.description: The text to type. It can hold escape sequences for keys that aren't text, such as \u001b[A for the up arrow.

bytes_written.description: The number of bytes queued, which is the length of data in UTF-8 bytes, not characters.

validation_notes: Call it as `com.superlogical.terminal.write` with `session_id`, `block_id`, and this method's own arguments under `args`.
